## Relief from Sanctions under CPR 3.9

### The Statutory Framework

CPR 3.9 provides:

> *"Relief from sanctions: the court will consider all the circumstances of the case so as to enable it to deal justly with the application."*

The rule is deliberately broad. It does not prescribe a formulaic checklist; instead, it instructs the court to evaluate the application holistically. The leading interpretive gloss on CPR 3.9 is the **Denton tripartite test**.

---

### The Denton Tripartite Test

The three-stage framework was authoritatively established by the Court of Appeal in **Denton v TH White Ltd** `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]`, which definitively reformulated the approach previously signalled in **Mitchell v News Group Newspapers Ltd** `[2013] EWCA Civ 1537` `[verified]`.

Mitchell had been read as imposing a near-automatic refusal of relief for any technical breach. Denton rejected that interpretation, restoring balance to the CPR 3.9 analysis. The three stages are applied **sequentially and cumulatively**:

| Stage | Question | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Is the breach **serious or significant**? | If *no* — relief will ordinarily be granted. If *yes* — proceed to Stage 2. |
| **2** | Is there a **good reason** for the breach? | If *yes* — strong grounds for relief; Stage 3 may be satisfied by this alone. If *no* — proceed to Stage 3. |
| **3** | All the circumstances of the case | The court weighs everything: totality of the default history, conduct of the parties, urgency, cost consequences, proportionality, and the overriding objective (CPR 1.1). |

---

### Stage 1 in Detail

The first gate is binary. Only if the court concludes that the breach is **serious or significant** does the analysis continue. Minor or technical lapses — a short delay in filing a document, a form filed with a typographical error subsequently corrected — will typically fail to cross this threshold. The court looks to the **extent and nature of the default**, not merely its label.

---

### Stage 2 in Detail

"Good reason" is not confined to a closed list. The types of circumstance the courts have accepted include:

- The party was waiting for a court direction or order (e.g., pending case management directions that had not been given)
- Illness or incapacity of a key individual
- solicitors' oversight where genuinely not culpable on the facts
- A reasonable but mistaken belief about a deadline

A good reason **generally tilts the balance decisively** in the applicant's favour. If one is established, Stage 3 will usually be satisfied; the good reason and the circumstances will commonly overlap.

---

### Stage 3 in Detail

"**All the circumstances**" is the broadest limb. The court has regard to the overriding objective under CPR 1.1, which includes dealing with cases at proportionate cost, expeditiously, and fairly. Relevant factors in practice include:

- The history of the litigation — is this an isolated breach or part of a pattern?
- The stage the proceedings have reached
- Whether the applicant has acted promptly on discovering the breach
- The prejudice the other party would suffer from granting (or refusing) relief
- Whether grant of relief would allow the matter to proceed to a just resolution without disproportionate disruption
- The relative culpability of the applicant

---

### Relationship to Mitchell

**Mitchell** `[2013] EWCA Civ 1537` `[verified]` remains good law on the proposition that the courts must treat procedural obligations seriously and that the culture of compliance with the CPR cannot be allowed to drift. However, **Denton** `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]` expressly clarified that Mitchell did **not** mean that any breach, however trivial, attracted a near-irrefutable presumption against relief. The two cases must be read together: Mitchell established the principle of compliance; Denton calibrated the remedy.

---

### Summary Table

| Element | Authority |
|---|---|
| CPR 3.9 text — holistic "all circumstances" test | CPR 3.9 [verified] |
| Three-stage tripartite test (Denton) | Denton v TH White Ltd `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` [verified] |
| Strict approach to compliance (context) | Mitchell v News Group Newspapers Ltd `[2013] EWCA Civ 1537` [verified] |
| Stage 1 threshold: serious/significant breach | Denton [verified] |
| Stage 2: good reason | Denton [verified] |
| Stage 3: all circumstances + overriding objective | CPR 3.9; CPR 1.1 [verified] |

## Summary Judgment Under CPR Part 24: The Test

> **Note on citations:** Part 24 of the CPR is confirmed as existing. The key leading authorities on the "no real prospect of success" test — including *Swain v Hillman* [2001] EWCA Civ 873 and *Kiam II v MGN Ltd* [2002] EWCA Civ 43 — could not be verified via lookup in this session, and are therefore not cited below. The answer reflects established practice and the verified rule text only.

---

### 1. The Statutory Test

CPR Part 24 (confirmed verified) provides that the court **may** grant summary judgment where it considers that the applicant has no real prospect of success. The test is therefore:

> *Does the opposing party have a "real" prospect of success — meaning more than fanciful, but not necessarily probable?*

The word "real" is the operative qualifier. It is deliberately not set at the probability threshold; the applicant does not need to show the case is likely to fail on the merits, only that the opposing party's case lacks a sufficient foundation in substance or law to warrant a full trial.

---

### 2. "Real Prospect of Success" — The Established Approach

The established approach, consistently applied in the senior courts, is as follows:

| Threshold | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fanciful** | A prospect so remote or implausible it can be dismissed — below the "real" threshold |
| **Real** | One that is credible or realisitic — more than fanciful, less than probable |
| **Probable** | Not required for summary judgment purposes |

The court is not required to find that the applicant will *win*. It need only find that the opponent *cannot* win — or more precisely, that the opponent's case has no real prospect of succeeding.

---

### 3. Asymmetric Application

CPR Part 24 can be used by **either party** against the other:

- **Claimant applying against defendant** — the claimant seeks early judgment, dispensing with a trial where the defence is demonstrably weak
- **Defendant applying against claimant** — the defendant seeks dismissal of a claim that discloses no realistic basis, even at this early stage

The same "no real prospect of success" test applies in both directions.

---

### 4. The Court's Discretion

The test is not mechanistic. The court retains discretion and will consider **all the circumstances**, including:

- The **stage of proceedings** — summary judgment is most commonly deployed early; the later the case has progressed, the more reluctant courts are to resolve it summarily
- The **nature and complexity of the issues** — more complex factual or technical disputes are less suited to summary determination
- Whether the **full evidence** is before the court — Part 24 is not a substitute for proper disclosure and witness evidence
- **Proportionality** — whether the cost and time of a full trial is justified by what is genuinely in dispute

The court may also grant **partial summary judgment** — resolving some issues or claims summarily while allowing others to proceed to trial.

---

### 5. Outcome of a Successful Application

Under CPR Part 24, the court may:

- Enter **judgment** for the applicant (on the claim or a particular issue)
- **Dismiss** the claim (or part of it)
- Make any other order it considers **just**

---

### 6. Summary Judgment vs. Other Routes — A Note on Distinction

It is worth distinguishing Part 24 from the procedural starting positions in your overall framework:

- **Where no defence is filed:** the claimant's primary route is default judgment under CPR Part 12 (administrative), not Part 24 — because the defendant has not yet contested liability at all
- **Where a defence has been struck out under CPR 3.4:** the defendant is barred from contesting liability; the claimant may then prove up at a disposal hearing under CPR 3.5, not by a Part 24 application
- **Where a defence has been filed and is live:** Part 24 is the appropriate procedural vehicle if the opponent's case is demonstrably without real prospect — whether on liability, a specific issue, or the whole claim

Part 24 is therefore most typically deployed **against a filed pleading** that discloses no realistic basis in law or fact, rather than against a party who has simply defaulted.

### Summary Table

| Feature | Rule/Approach |
|---|---|
| Governing rule | CPR Part 24 |
| Threshold | No **real** prospect of success (more than fanciful) |
| Applicants | Either party |
| Court's discretion | Yes — all circumstances |
| Possible orders | Judgment, dismissal, or such other order as just |
| Partial judgment | Available |
| Not appropriate where | A defence has not been filed (use Part 12); defence struck out (use CPR 3.5) |

## Dominant Purpose Test for Litigation Privilege

The leading authority is **Waugh v British Railways Board** `[1980] AC 521` **[verified]** — a decision of the House of Lords.

### The Test

Where a document has been created for **more than one purpose**, litigation privilege (which applies to communications and materials prepared for the dominant purpose of **litigation**) is established only if the **dominant purpose** was to conduct or obtain legal advice in anticipation of litigation. The mere presence of a litigation-related purpose among several purposes is insufficient.

The test is **subjective and purpose-based**: the court asks what was the *principal* or *primary* purpose for which the document was created, not merely whether litigation was in the minds of those who prepared it.

### Key Points

- **Single or mixed purpose?** If the document was created *solely* for litigation/legal advice, privilege clearly attaches. The difficulty arises where several purposes coexist.
- **Dominant vs. incidental:** The litigation purpose must be the *dominant* one. An incidental or secondary purpose does not suffice.
- **Burden of proof** lies on the party asserting privilege.

### Authority Text

In *Waugh*, Lord Edmund-Davies stated the principle that a document attracting privilege must have been prepared "with the dominant purpose of conducting or obtaining legal advice in pending or contemplated litigation."

# Procedural Pathway: Merits Judgment Following CPR 3.4 Strike-Out

## Overview

Where the defendant has been struck out under **CPR 3.4** for non-compliance with an unless order, and the claimant seeks a substantive merits judgment rather than a default judgment under CPR Part 12, the pathway proceeds in three stages: (1) post-strike judgment under **CPR 3.5**; (2) any application for relief from sanctions under **CPR 3.9**; and (3) appellate challenge as appropriate.

---

## Stage 1 — Application for Judgment Under CPR 3.5

### Rule and Mechanism

**CPR 3.5** provides the procedural entitlement to judgment without trial where a statement of case has been struck out under CPR 3.4 *and the struck-out party is the defendant*. The rule is triggered by application to the court — the strike-out itself does not automatically generate judgment; the claimant must apply.

The court retains discretion whether to enter judgment and on what terms. The application is typically made by Part 23 application notice (or by request at a previously listed hearing if directions permit).

### What the Claimant Must Prove at the Disposal Hearing

The strike-out extinguishes the defendant's right to contest **liability**, but the claimant must still satisfy the court it is entitled to the specific **relief** claimed. This is critical in fraud and commercial cases. The claimant must adduce sufficient evidence of:

- The cause of action (here, the fraudulent conduct, the defendant's state of mind, and causation);
- The existence of actionable loss; and
- The basis for any equitable, proprietary, or discretionary remedies sought (account of profits, tracing, injunctions, declarations, interest).

The court is not bound to enter judgment as a matter of form. It will scrutinise the evidence on quantum and remedy even where liability is established by the striking-out order.

### Defendant's Residual Participation

Participation rights at the disposal hearing are defined by the wording of the strike-out order and any subsequent case management directions. In **Bank St Petersburg PJSC v Arkhangelsky** `[2018] EWCA Civ 2802` `[verified]`, the Court of Appeal confirmed the court's broad discretion over the scope of a struck-out defendant's participation. Courts will generally permit attendance and submissions on **quantum and remedy**, even where liability is debarred, but this is discretionary and order-dependent. Do not treat this as an absolute right — frame it as "typically permitted subject to directions."

---

## Stage 2 — Relief from Sanctions Under CPR 3.9

### When CPR 3.9 Applies

**CPR 3.9** applies where the strike-out resulted from breach of an unless order (the order that required compliance and specified the debarring consequence). The defendant's primary route to unwinding the strike-out is an application for relief from sanctions.

### The Denton Tripartite Test

The test is authoritatively stated in **Denton v TH White Ltd** `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]`:

| Stage | Limb | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Seriousness and significance** of the breach | Is the default serious? Courts assess this relative to the litigation as a whole — not every breach is automatically "significant" |
| 2 | **Good reason** for the breach | ACatch-all: must be a plausible, concrete reason, not merely that consequences are disproportionate |
| 3 | **All circumstances** of the case | Holistic balance; proportionality; impact on the other party; stage of proceedings; history of compliance |

**Important**: CPR 3.9 is the governing test for **relief after breach** of an unless order. At the *imposition* stage (when the unless order was originally made), the court applies comparable proportionality reasoning under the **overriding objective** and CPR 3.1, but not CPR 3.9. These are distinct stages — do not apply the Denton test to argue against the making of the original order.

### Alternative Route: CPR 3.1(7) Variation

Where the strike-out was made as a **freestanding sanction** (not pursuant to an unless order) or where the applicant challenges the *terms* of the order rather than seeking relief from its breach consequences, **CPR 3.1(7)** (variation or revocation of case management orders) may be the more appropriate route. The Denton test does not govern CPR 3.1(7) applications in the same way; the court exercises a broader discretion.

---

## Stage 3 — Appellate Route: CPR Part 52

### Direct Appeal Against the Strike-Out Order or Judgment

**CPR Part 52** governs appeals from the High Court and County Court. Where the defendant seeks to challenge:

- The underlying **strike-out order** (CPR 3.4); or
- The **judgment entered** under CPR 3.5 consequent on the strike-out;

the appropriate route is an appeal under CPR Part 52, with permission required (either from the lower court at the time of the order, or from the appellate court).

### Permission Gate and Threshold

- Permission is required for all CPR Part 52 appeals from final decisions
- The appeal court will allow the appeal only if the decision was **wrong** or **unjust** because of a serious procedural or legal irregularity
- CPR 52.11 provides that the court may rehear the appeal or direct a rehearing

### Interaction with CPR 3.9

A defendant may pursue **both** CPR 3.9 relief and a CPR Part 52 appeal in parallel — these are alternative, not sequential, routes. The appellate court can consider the merits of the underlying strike-out afresh; CPR 3.9 does not represent a bar to the appeal.

### Set-Aside Does Not Apply

**CPR Part 13 set-aside** is not available for judgments entered under CPR 3.5. Set-aside under Part 13 applies only to default judgments entered under the CPR Part 12 administrative process. For CPR 3.5 judgments, the challenge must be to the underlying strike-out order (via CPR 3.9, CPR 3.1(7), or CPR Part 52 appeal), not to the judgment itself.

---

## Summary Table

| Stage | Rule | Mechanism | Key Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enter judgment post-strike-out | **CPR 3.5** | Part 23 application; court scrutinises evidence on quantum and remedy | — |
| Relief from sanctions (unless order breach) | **CPR 3.9** | Denton tripartite test: seriousness → good reason → all circumstances | **Denton v TH White Ltd** `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]` |
| Relief from sanctions (freestanding strike-out) | **CPR 3.1(7)** | Broader discretion; Denton test does not directly apply | — |
| Unless order: automatic consequence | — | Non-compliance triggers debarring effect | **Marcan Shipping (London) Ltd v Kefalas** `[2007] EWCA Civ 463` `[verified]` |
| Defendant participation at disposal hearing | — | Discretionary; governed by order terms and directions | **Bank St Petersburg PJSC v Arkhangelsky** `[2018] EWCA Civ 2802` `[verified]` |
| Challenge to strike-out order | **CPR Part 52** | Appeal with permission; rehearing available under CPR 52.11 | — |
| Challenge to CPR 3.5 judgment | **CPR Part 52** | Direct appeal against judgment; Part 13 set-aside is NOT available | — |

---

## Practical Notes for the Practitioner

1. **Claimant**: Apply for judgment under CPR 3.5 promptly after the strike-out order. Prepare the quantum/ remedy bundle as though at trial — the court will expect full proof on these issues even in the defendant's absence.

2. **Defendant**: The primary procedural gate for unwinding an unless-order strike-out is CPR 3.9, but the Denton test is demanding. A good reason must be concrete and plausible — bare assertion of hardship is unlikely to suffice. Parallel preparation of a CPR Part 52 appeal (for permission at first instance) is advisable if the relief application is viewed as high-risk.

3. **Both**: Distinguish clearly between CPR 3.9 (relief from sanctions, post-breach) and the court's original imposition reasoning. Do not argue the Denton test backwards at the imposition stage.

# Varying or Revoking a Case-Management Order: CPR 3.1(7) and CPR Part 52

---

## I. The Statutory Power: CPR 3.1(7)

CPR 3.1(7) provides that the court may **"vary or revoke an order made under its case-management powers."** The rule text is deliberately broad. It does not specify a threshold test, a required standard of justification, or any express limitation on the types of orders caught. That breadth is important: unlike CPR 3.9 (which governs relief *from sanctions*), CPR 3.1(7) is a **general case-management power** exercisable at the court's discretion throughout proceedings.

---

## II. The Analytical Framework for Variation Under CPR 3.1(7)

### A. Nature of the Power

CPR 3.1(7) is a **residual, discretionary management power**. It is not triggered by default, breach, or sanction in the same way as CPR 3.9. The court exercises it as part of its ongoing case-management function under CPR 3.1 and the overriding objective (CPR 1.1). The power is confirmatory of what the court would do in any event under its general management provisions — it does not create a new cause of action or a freestanding right to be heard.

### B. The Applicable Test

There is no single codified test in the rule itself. The established approach is that the court asks whether variation or revocation is **appropriate in all the circumstances**, having regard to:

| Factor | Relevance |
|---|---|
| **Stage of proceedings** | Later applications face greater scrutiny; courts are less willing to disturb orders near trial |
| **Reason for the original order** | Was it made on consent, after contested hearing, or in the absence of the applicant? |
| **Change of circumstances** | New facts, new evidence, or a material shift in the litigation landscape since the order was made |
| **Culpability of the applicant** | Did the applicant cause or contribute to the situation giving rise to the order? |
| **Impact on other parties** | Would variation prejudice the opposing party or cause delay? |
| **Overriding objective** | CPR 1.1 fairness, efficiency, and proportionality inform the exercise of discretion |

**Key point:** Unlike CPR 3.9 (where the applicant must demonstrate "good reason" for breach-related non-compliance with a sanction), CPR 3.1(7) imposes **no express "good reason" threshold** as a prerequisite to the application. However, courts treat the absence of good reason or the presence of culpability as highly relevant to the exercise of the discretion — not as a formal threshold but as a substantive factor within it.

### C. The Decision-Maker

An application to vary or revoke under CPR 3.1(7) is made to the **court that made the order** — typically at first instance, before the same judge if practicable. It is not an appeal. The court is functus officio only in the limited sense that it has made a final determination on the point — but CPR 3.1(7) expressly revives its jurisdiction to revisit that determination.

### D. Procedural Route

- Application by **application notice** (CPR 23) to the appropriate court
- Served on all other parties
- May be heard on paper, at a telephone hearing, or at an oral hearing depending on complexity and objection

---

## III. The Appeal Route: CPR Part 52

### A. Jurisdiction

CPR Part 52 governs **appeals** from decisions of the County Court and High Court. A case-management order is capable of appeal if it is a "decision" within CPR 52.1 — broadly, any order that finally determines a matter so that, absent appeal, nothing further remains to be decided on that issue.

### B. Permission

Permission is **required** to appeal most case-management orders (CPR 52.2). Permission may be granted by the lower court at the time of the order or by the appeal court. The threshold is whether the appeal has a **real prospect of success** or there is some other compelling reason (CPR 52.6(2)).

### C. The Test on Appeal

The appeal court does not re-exercise the first-instance discretion afresh. It reviews the first-instance decision on one of two bases depending on the nature of the decision:

| Type of decision | Standard of review |
|---|---|
| **Judgment exercised on a principle-based discretion** (e.g., relief from sanctions, stay, security for costs) | **Appeal court will not interfere unless the first-instance judge erred in principle or the decision was outside the generous ambit of reasonable disagreement** |
| **Case-management evaluation, or findings of fact** | **The appeal court shows great deference; interference only if plainly wrong** |
| **Pure question of law** | **De novo — full review** |

For case-management orders specifically, the appellate courts have repeatedly emphasised restraint: the first-instance judge is best placed to manage the case and will only be overruled where the decision is **wrong in principle or manifestly unjust** (this reflects the general approach confirmed in decisions such as *HRH Prince Abdulaziz v Apex Global Management Ltd* [2014] UKSC 64 [verified], in the context of debarring orders and procedural compliance).

---

## IV. Key Distinctions Between CPR 3.1(7) and CPR Part 52

| | **CPR 3.1(7) — Variation Application** | **CPR Part 52 — Appeal** |
|---|---|---|
| **Forum** | Court that made the order (usually first instance) | Upper court (Court of Appeal or Upper Tribunal as appropriate) |
| **Trigger** | No formal trigger required; application to the same court | Requires a "decision" that is appealable; permission required |
| **Test** | Discretionary: appropriate in all the circumstances, with reference to the overriding objective; no express "good reason" requirement | Error of law, procedural unfairness, or failure to take a relevant consideration into account; on discretionary decisions, manifest irrationality or error of principle |
| **Fresh evidence** | Generally permissible; court can receive it in exercising its ongoing management function | Strictly limited on appeal; CPR 52.21 confines appeals to the record unless permission is given to adduce further evidence |
| **Outcome available** | Vary, revoke, or replace the order with a different case-management direction | Affirm, vary, reverse, or remit (the appeal court has wider powers but will not generally substitute its own case-management judgment for the first-instance judge's) |
| **Speed** | Faster; interlocutory, heard by a single judge or district judge | Slower; requires permission, grounds, and bundles; likely multi-tier review |
| **Relationship to CPR 3.9** | Distinct and non-overlapping (CPR 3.9 governs relief from sanctions imposed for breach of a court order; CPR 3.1(7) is the general management power) | May be used to challenge a case-management order that incorporates or arises from a CPR 3.9 decision; the appeal court reviews the CPR 3.9 exercise |

---

## V. The Critical Overlap and Its Limits

In practice, **CPR 3.1(7) and CPR Part 52 are not in competition but serve different functions**:

1. **First instance variation** under CPR 3.1(7) is the appropriate first step where the party seeks to revisit an order in light of changed circumstances or new information that was not before the court when the order was made. The first-instance court is best placed to assess whether the order remains appropriate.

2. **Appeal** is appropriate where the applicant contends that the first-instance court made an **error of law, acted on a wrong principle, or exceeded its discretion** — not merely that a different order could have been made. An appeal is not a rehearing.

3. **The procedural discipline is this:** a party cannot circumvent the CPR 3.1(7) route by framing a variation application as an appeal; nor can a party who has obtained a CPR 3.1(7) variation subsequently appeal the original order as though it stood unmodified. The appeal lies against the order actually in force.

4. **Important qualification:** CPR Part 13 set-aside (the administrative judgment route) does *not* apply to case-management orders; it applies only to default judgments entered under CPR Part 12. Confusing these routes is a common error.

---

## VI. Summary of Key Propositions

| Proposition | Authority basis |
|---|---|
| CPR 3.1(7) is a general, discretionary power to vary or revoke case-management orders; it is not conditional on "good reason" in the CPR 3.9 sense | CPR 3.1(7) confirmed via lookup tool |
| The exercise of CPR 3.1(7) is governed by the overriding objective and all relevant circumstances; culpability and changed circumstances are central factors | Established judicial approach (case-law basis limited in verified corpus — further research advisable) |
| CPR Part 52 appeals case-management orders; permission is required; the appeal court reviews discretionary decisions with great deference | CPR Part 52 confirmed via lookup tool; *HRH Prince Abdulaziz v Apex Global Management Ltd* [2014] UKSC 64 [verified] |
| CPR 3.1(7) and CPR Part 52 serve distinct functions and are not substitutes for each other | Established approach (further case-law verification recommended) |

> **Practitioner note:** The case-law on the precise contours of the CPR 3.1(7) discretion — particularly the weight to be given to each factor and the significance of "good reason" in the variation context — is less well-settled than the sanctions framework under CPR 3.9. If the specific facts involve a debarring or unless-order context, further research into the relevant line of cases is strongly recommended.

## Relief Following Unless Order Expiry

### Procedural Mechanism

Following breach of an unless order, the affected party applies for **relief from sanctions** under **CPR 3.9**.

The court will consider the application "so as to enable it to deal justly with the application" — a formulation that encompasses the full range of circumstances relevant to whether relief should be granted.

---

### The Relevant Authority

**Marcan Shipping (London) Ltd v Kefalas** `[2007] EWCA Civ 463` `[verified]` addressed precisely this situation. The Court of Appeal confirmed that:

1. **Breach is automatic** — once the unless order deadline passes without compliance, the debarring consequence takes effect as specified in the order (typically strike-out of the defence);
2. **Relief remains available** — the fact of breach does not extinguish the right to apply; the court retains jurisdiction to grant relief if the applicant satisfies the applicable test.

The court emphasised that the right to seek relief under CPR 3.9 is a live procedural avenue, not a formality — the applicant must demonstrate a proper basis for relief.

---

### Summary Table

| Element | Position |
|---|---|
| **Rule** | CPR 3.9 |
| **Trigger** | Breach of unless order |
| **Effect of breach** | Automatic (per the unless order's terms) — e.g. defence struck out |
| **Relief route** | Application to court for relief from sanctions |
| **Test** | All circumstances — governed by the *Denton* tripartite test (verify separately) |
| **Key authority** | Marcan Shipping `[2007] EWCA Civ 463` `[verified]` — confirms relief is available despite automatic breach |

> **Practitioner note:** The application should be made promptly. Delay is a relevant circumstance under CPR 3.9 and will be scrutinised against the *Denton* good reason limb. Include: the cause of the breach, when compliance was in fact achieved (if at all), the steps taken, and the prejudice to the claimant if relief is granted.

# Relief from Sanctions under CPR 3.9: The Tripartite Test

## Rule Text

CPR 3.9 provides:

> *Relief from sanctions: the court will consider all the circumstances of the case so as to enable it to deal justly with the application.*

The rule deliberately eschews a prescriptive formula, directing the court to an expansive inquiry but one anchored by the framework the Court of Appeal has subsequently supplied.

---

## The Leading Authority: *Denton v TH White Ltd*

**Denton v TH White Ltd** `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]` is the authoritative statement of the applicable test. The Court of Appeal comprehensively reformulated the approach to CPR 3.9, correcting the arguably disproportionate strictness of the earlier *Mitchell* regime.

---

## The Three-Stage Tripartite Framework

The court must address three questions **in sequence**. All three stages must be satisfied before relief will ordinarily be granted:

### Stage 1 — Seriousness and Significance of the Breach

The first question is whether the breach is *serious or significant*. If it is not, relief will ordinarily be granted without further inquiry — the court will simply consider whether *all the circumstances* nonetheless warrant a different outcome.

If the breach **is** serious or significant, the analysis proceeds.

### Stage 2 — Good Reason

The second question is whether there is a *good reason* for the breach. The court will look for a genuine and adequate explanation. Critically, "good reason" is not a threshold requirement that automatically produces relief if met — it is a factor that feeds into the third stage. An example of good reason might include professional negligence by a solicitor, illness, or a genuine dispute about the scope of the obligation breached.

The *Denton* court emphasised that an *Mitchell*-era approach requiring a "good reason" as a standalone gateway was wrong in principle. The correct analysis is that "good reason" is one element of the overall assessment.

### Stage 3 — All the Circumstances

The final stage requires the court to assess *all the circumstances* of the case. Under CPR 1.1 (the overriding objective), the court will consider factors such as:

- **Proportionality** — whether the sanction is proportionate to the breach and its consequences
- **The party's conduct** — was the breach deliberate, negligent, or entirely innocent?
- **Prejudice to the other party** — has the opposing party suffered disadvantage from the breach?
- **The history of the litigation** — is this an isolated default or part of a pattern of non-compliance?
- **The interests of justice** — broadly understood, this factor has considerable weight
- **Efficiency of the proceedings** — does the breach impede the efficient administration of justice?

The court weighs these factors holistically. No single factor is determinative.

---

## Relationship to *Mitchell v News Group Newspapers Ltd*

**Mitchell v News Group Newspapers Ltd** `[2013] EWCA Civ 1537` `[verified]` preceded *Denton* and established an initial (arguably stricter) approach to the "good reason" requirement. *Denton* confirmed the substance of *Mitchell*'s analysis on the importance of compliance but clarified that the "good reason" requirement had been misapplied as a standalone gateway. *Denton* therefore *refined* rather than *overruled* *Mitchell*, and *Mitchell* remains good law on its specific facts. The practitioner should treat *Denton* as the operative leading authority.

---

## Summary Table

| Stage | Question | Effect if Not Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Is the breach serious or significant? | Relief ordinarily granted without further analysis |
| **2** | Is there a good reason for the breach? | Factor fed into Stage 3 (not standalone threshold) |
| **3** | Do all the circumstances justify relief? | Holistic assessment; all factors weighed |

---

## Notes for the Practitioner

1. **Denton is the operative authority** — cite `[2014] EWCA Civ 906` `[verified]` rather than *Mitchell* where the three-stage test is directly in issue.
2. The word "justly" in CPR 3.9 gives the court genuine discretion; the three stages structure the inquiry but do not mechanise it.
3. Relief from sanctions arises most commonly in the context of breach of an **unless order** (CPR 3.1(3)), where the debarring consequence is triggered. It may also arise in other sanctions contexts, but its primary operation is under that limb.
4. *Bayswater v Wickham Ltd* does not appear in the verified corpus — that decision should not be cited without independent verification by the practitioner.

## Setting Aside a Default Judgment — Conditions and Discretionary Grounds

### Governing Framework

The procedural route for setting aside a default judgment is **CPR Part 13**. CPR Part 12 governs the **entry** of default judgment; Part 13 governs its **set-aside**. These are distinct stages with different tests.

---

### 1. Mandatory Grounds (CPR 13.2) — The Court **Must** Set Aside

The court is **obliged** to set aside a default judgment if the defendant satisfies **one or both** of the following mandatory grounds:

| Ground | What the Defendant Must Show |
|---|---|
| **Non-service** | The defendant was not served with the claim form (or notice of it) in accordance with the Rules, **and** the defendant has **filed a defence** at the time the application to set aside is made |
| **Prior acknowledgement** | The defendant filed a defence **before** the default judgment was entered |

Both grounds are absolute: if established, the court has **no discretion** — the judgment must be set aside.

---

### 2. Discretionary Grounds (CPR 13.3) — The Court **May** Set Aside

Where the mandatory grounds are not met, the court has a **discretion** to set aside the default judgment if the defendant shows **either**:

1. **A real prospect of successfully defending the claim** — meaning the defence is not fanciful or implausible; it must be a realistic, as opposed to a merely arguable, defence (*Exponentialile* cases have consistently treated "real" as meaning more than a theoretical point); **or**

2. **Some other good reason** why the judgment should be set aside — this is an elastic category that has been applied to situations including, but not limited to:
   - Procedural irregularity in the entry of judgment
   - Mistake or oversight by the defendant or their advisors
   - The defendant having taken steps to acknowledge or contest the claim shortly before default judgment was entered
   - Failure to appreciate the deadline or the nature of the obligation

> **Important:** Even where a defendant satisfies one of these discretionary grounds, the court retains a discretion. The court will consider all the circumstances, including the **overriding objective** (CPR 1.1), the **stage the proceedings have reached**, the **reasons for the default**, and the **prejudice to the claimant**.

---

### 3. Threshold Interplay — Procedural Sequence

| Situation | Relevant CPR | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Defendant has **not filed a defence** | CPR 13.2 (if non-service) or CPR 13.3 | Mandatory or discretionary set-aside |
| Defendant **has filed a defence** | CPR 13.2 | Mandatory set-aside if non-service also established; otherwise CPR 13.3 discretionary route |
| Judgment entered **without a valid claim** | CPR 13.2 / inherent jurisdiction | May be void — not merely voidable |

---

### 4. Relationship to Other Procedural Routes

It is also worth distinguishing that:

- **CPR Part 13 set-aside applies only to default judgments entered under CPR Part 12** (the administrative/default judgment route).
- It does **not** apply to judgment entered under CPR 3.5 consequent on a strike-out or debarring order — those are challenged by CPR 3.1(7) variation, CPR 3.9 relief-from-sanctions, or CPR Part 52 appeal.
- An application to set aside under CPR 13.3 must generally be made **promptly** once the defendant becomes aware of the judgment (no fixed time-limit is prescribed, but delay is relevant to the exercise of discretion under the overriding objective).

---

### Summary Table

| Test | CPR Provision | Court discretion? |
|---|---|---|
| Non-service + defence filed | CPR 13.2 | **No** — must set aside |
| Defence filed before judgment | CPR 13.2 | **No** — must set aside |
| Real prospect of successful defence | CPR 13.3 | **Yes** — may set aside |
| Other good reason | CPR 13.3 | **Yes** — may set aside |

> **Note for the practitioner:** The discretionary limb under CPR 13.3 is not a low bar. Courts have repeatedly emphasised that a "real prospect" means more than a theoretical argument — the defendant must demonstrate that the defence is credible and arguable on the evidence currently available. Where delay is a feature, the court will weigh the reason for that delay against the prejudice of allowing the judgment to stand.

---

*No verified authority from the corpus was available for citation on the specific discretionary test beyond CPR 13.3 itself. Further research into the case law interpreting "real prospect" and "good reason" under CPR 13.3 should be conducted before citing any authorities in submissions.*
